replies.text:
The human mind strives for change or novelty of any kind, hence the hallucinations induced when you've looked at the same thing for any amount of time. If you stare expressionlessly at your own face in the mirror, it will eventually distort (this happens faster in the dark), and I imagine that dreams are the same kind of experiential phenomena that exist to prevent us from experiencing sameness for too long, even if it's just lying with our eyes closed.

To geek out for a second, this part of the human condition is why I love meditating so much. Meditation is a direct challenge to this strive for novelty by way of integrating mindful observation and bodily stillness without striving for dreams or hallucinations, chasing specific thoughts or emotions, or even engaging in self-talk. Philosophically, there's a strange sense of comfort in recognizing that there's always something there, even in the most solitary of darkness — consciousness.

The fear of the dark comes from the fear that an unknown, unknowable "other" presence could be concealed within it. With Michael's experience, he knew that no other presence was in the room with him because he could see, but in the dark, there's no frame of reference to denote that anything else is there.

Here's a thought experiment: Would you rather consciously stay in prolonged light or darkness? I think I'd actually prefer prolonged darkness — my only stipulation is that it not be cold. Calling back to 'Fear of Cold,' this is a more impactful fear that affects me. Dark without cold? Totally fine. Dark and cold? That's something I'm not fond of thinking about, lol.

As a child, I once stumbled across a "Japanese urban legend". I've long since forgotten where I heard it, it may not even be Japanese at all. It was titled "The girl in the gap". replies.author: @SirLightsOut99
replies.text: Hi! Completely blind person here. I'm gonna do my best to explain my perceptions of darkness to the best of my abilities. I guess technically I don't understand true dark. Of course when it's dark outside I know, but how dark it is is a mystery. To me, the dark is more about sound, and feeling, and the absence of movement that you get in the light. I've lived in big cities and out in the middle of nowhere, and while the environment changes, the vibe does not. All the birds, the cars driving by, all that grows a lot quieter, or on the worst nights disappears  entirely. It's never been the dark that freaks me out, it's the quiet that comes with it. A quiet day out in my neck of the woods is fine. You still have the sounds of nature around you, maybe you catch the neighbors making some kind of noise, maybe the dogs are barking off in the distance. It's quiet, but not silent. Nights here are a different beast though, at least at their worst. When I'm out with people, it's fine. There's talking, there's sound, there's something to cut through the nothing. But there's some nights when I'm asked to go out and grab something, and it's just dead silent out there. None of the frogs or crickets that usually populate the night, no birds, no rumbling from our house's Ac or heating, no cars driving by, nothing. That's when I'm really on edge. I swear to you, if it's quiet enough, silence is a sound unto itself and it is weirdly oppressive. When you live your life accustomed to sound, having all of it taken away is just as disorienting as not being able to see. It's scary dude. And it all comes back to that central idea: either it's just you in that silence, or there's something else there that you don't know about. You start thinking you hear things, whether they're there or they aren't, because you're supposed to hear things, and you not hearing things just feels wrong. It makes me feel a bit vulnerable, but it's also weirdly beautiful. Like in a world that's often so noisy, walking in an area where there's just nothing is kinda cool in a strange way. It makes things feel like they've never been tampered with, like it's just the natural order of the world. Maybe that doesn't make any sense, I don't know, but depending on the day's events, the temperature outside, all kinds of factors honestly, that crushing silence can be peaceful, or a driving source to get myself back into the house ASAP. Maybe this all sounds really wordy and pretentious, maybe the English major in me is coming out a little bit here, but that's honestly how it is.

topComment.author: @FrizzlenillCAN
topComment.text: Charles Bonnet syndrome is the name for when these hallucinations happen after physical vision loss - it's similar to phantom limb, where the brain regions responsible for receiving sensory input start firing disorganizedly when that input is fully lost (normally there's a baseline "nothing's happening" signal that keeps things organized in the conventional absence of sensory data). Oliver Sacks wrote a fair bit about these types of hallucinations, how these regions of the brain eventually get 'bored' and start firing without specific structure, and then later brain areas interpret that signalling the same way as any other sensory signal that would be passed to them. Phantom limb is this kind of hallucination for proprioceptive and tactile information - charles bonnet syndrome is the same, for partial or complete vision loss, and can involve highly complex and detailed imagery without even dream logic to cohere it together.

Strangely, one of the first games I ever played that made me think keenly about the dark was, of all things, Metroid II for the original Gameboy. Rendered on that tiny colorless screen, its simplified renditions of the environment of SR388 are set against an ever-present black backdrop that felt pressingly isolating, perfectly complimenting the grim mission Samus was sent there to accomplish, an express genocide of the Metroid species. For whatever reason, something about that lightless expanse felt infinitely deep, the simple absence of color managing to evoke the immeasurable void of space. The game's progression through the world is largely charted by delving further below the planet's surface, and the winding maze-like map layout helps obscure the sense of how far you've traveled, creating the impression of a labyrinthine descent into unknowable depths. It's not a game that was scary in the traditional sense, but I felt a heaviness to its atmosphere as I played it.

I've mentioned my experience with Metroid II to others I know who have played it, all of whom have said they never really felt the same way about it, with one even remarking essentially "old graphics like that are more about what you bring to them". And that feels kind of true of darkness as a whole. Given that it's arguably nothing at all, it can only be defined by how the person experiencing the dark perceives it.

My best friend and I went to see Skinamarink in theaters two years ago. It was january and our showing was at 7:15 pm, so it was pitch black when we arrived and when we got out of the movie. I have never been particularly afraid of the dark, but the way that movie taps into the primal childhood fear made me dread going home to the darkness of my house, where everyone else was already in bed. Laying in bed trying to go to sleep, I couldn't figure out if it was better or worse to keep my eyes on my bedroom door, which I leave slightly open for my cat to go in and out, and my closet, which has no door at all. Neither of them bother me normally, but that night they were portals to an abyss that the glow of the fairy lights over my windows couldn't touch. There was no solid form to my unease, Skinamarink doesn't ever let you see the thing that torments the children, so my mind had no face to latch onto. But SOMETHING was a possibility to the lizard part of my brain. I am not generally afraid of the dark, but on the occasions when I am, that question is always close at hand: is there nothing there, or is there something there?

Fantastic essay as always. I always appreciate that the "Fear Of" videos go so much deeper than just "this is scary because it is." This one put into words perfectly the faceless fear that I've felt from the dark.
